title: Depth Control of Room-Temperature Quantum Emitters in Gallium Nitride
authors: Alexandros Bampis, Johann Stachurski, Anna Schwab, Jean-François Carlin, Raphaël Butté, Nicolas Grandjean
abstract: Bright quantum emitters are key components for quantum communication systems. Radiative point defects in gallium nitride (GaN) are promising candidates for room-temperature single-photon emission, operating from the visible to the telecom O-band. Despite their potential, their integration into photonic structures has remained limited in the literature, with experimental photon extraction efficiencies far below simulated predictions. To identify the origin of this limitation, we investigate visible and near-infrared quantum emitters in GaN epilayers grown on $c$-plane sapphire substrates exhibiting narrow linewidths ($\sim$4 nm), high photon count rates ($ > $2 MHz), and strong antibunching, reaching $g^{(2)}(0)$ values as low as 0.06 at room temperature. We find that these emitters are located near the GaN/substrate interface, explaining their limited coupling to optical modes. Building on this observation, we show that the insertion of a thin low-temperature GaN interlayer enables the formation of quantum emitters at arbitrary depths with sub-60 nm accuracy, independent of the substrate. The intentionally introduced emitters retain optical properties comparable to naturally occurring ones, including narrow linewidths ($\sim$6 nm), saturation count rates exceeding 1.5 MHz, high Debye-Waller factors (0.69-0.98), and strong antibunching. The resulting epilayer fully coalesces within less than 250 nm ensuring compatibility with GaN-based cavity fabrication and enabling emitter placement within intrinsic regions of p-i-n diode architectures. These results mark a decisive step toward efficient emitter-cavity coupling, enabling the realization of cavity-enhanced quantum emission in GaN.
summary: This paper reports a major advance in solid-state quantum emitters by demonstrating precise, depth-controlled placement of bright quantum emitters in Gallium Nitride. By engineering the growth process using a low-temperature interlayer, the authors overcome the natural limitation of emitters being stuck at the substrate interface. This capability is crucial for realizing efficient, cavity-enhanced quantum light sources for quantum technologies.
main_problem: The primary challenge is the poor integration of bright, room-temperature quantum emitters (QEs) in Gallium Nitride (GaN) into functional photonic structures due to their natural location near the substrate interface.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a breakthrough by using a low-temperature GaN interlayer to precisely control the placement of QEs at arbitrary depths within the epilayer, enabling efficient coupling to optical cavities.
method: The study combines advanced micro-photoluminescence ($\mu$-PL) mapping, depth-resolved spectroscopy, and epitaxial growth engineering (using low-temperature interlayers) to physically manipulate and characterize the emitters.
model_or_system: The physical system is radiative point defects acting as single-photon emitters within GaN epilayers grown on sapphire. The methodology involves controlling the growth process (e.g., introducing a low-temperature GaN interlayer) to dictate the physical location of these defects.
key_observables: Narrow linewidths ($\sim 4-6$ nm), high photon count rates ($> 2$ MHz), strong antibunching ($g^{(2)}(0) \le 0.06$), and precise depth control (sub-60 nm accuracy).
important_parameters: Room temperature operation, visible to telecom O-band emission, and the ability to place emitters independent of the substrate material.
main_assumptions: The optical properties of the intentionally introduced QEs are assumed to be comparable to naturally occurring ones, and the depth profiling relies on empirical matching to structural measurements (SEM/SIMS).
figures_summary: Figures show $\mu$-PL maps confirming emitter localization, depth-resolved XZ PL maps demonstrating depth control, and spectra confirming high-quality single-photon emission characteristics.
paper_structure: The work progresses from identifying the initial limitation (interface confinement) to developing an engineering solution (LT interlayer deposition) and finally confirming the success of this method by showing depth-tunable, high-quality emitters compatible with cavity fabrication.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of coupling solid-state quantum emitters to optical cavities, which is a cornerstone problem in quantum optics and quantum information processing. The precise depth control mechanism is highly relevant for designing integrated quantum photonic circuits.
